A named MS and Neuroimmunology Center with five physicians, a research chair and an in-house fellowship. The center sits inside the Mulva Clinic for the Neurosciences (endowed by a $50 million Mulva Family Foundation gift) and is staffed by Leorah Freeman, M.D., Ph.D.; Duriel Hardy, M.D.; Esther Melamed, M.D., Ph.D.; Ethan Meltzer, M.D.; and Navid Valizadeh, M.B., BCh. Melamed is Associate Chair for Research for the department, founded the MS and Neuroimmunology Clinic at Dell Seton, runs the Melamed Lab on genetic, environmental and sex differences in MS, and directs research for UT Medicine's Post-COVID-19 Program. Freeman works on advanced imaging of MS disability progression and created the Moving Stronger exercise program with the YMCA and the Texas chapter of the National MS Society. The Directors' Welcome confirms the department 'currently offers fellowships in neurophysiology, neuroimmunology and vascular neurology' - she could subspecialise in neuroimmunology without leaving Austin.

The residency continuity clinic and the Seton Infusion Center are in the same building. Residents follow their own patient panel from PGY-2 through PGY-4 at the Health Transformation Building, and 'The Seton Infusion Center is also in the HTB, which allows for many neurology patients who require outpatient infusions to receive treatment there.' For someone whose interest is MS, that means following her own MS patients through disease-modifying infusion therapy in her own clinic building across three years, rather than referring them away.

A published Step 2 CK preference of 200, not 230 or 240. The program's FAQ states 'A score of 200 or higher on the first attempt on Step II is preferred', and no source I could verify publishes any higher bar. Combined with the FREIDA survey's field_usmle_step2_req_int = false, this is a program whose published rules do not punish a mid-October score. For an applicant whose Step 2 result arrives after ERAS review begins, that combination is rare and valuable.

A named PGY-4 movement disorder rotation at the institute her program is named after, with fellowship-trained specialists and DBS. The Curriculum page lists 'additional outpatient offerings such as epilepsy and movement disorder rotations' among new senior-resident rotations, and describes the Ascension Seton Brain & Spine Institute as staffed by 'an array of neurologists with different subspecialities, including epileptologists, clinical neurophysiologists and movement disorder specialists', where residents also learn EMG/NCV and botulinum toxin injections. Erik Z. Krause, D.O. at that institute is movement-disorders fellowship-trained with DBS programming and botulinum toxin. Ascension offers DBS for movement disorders in Austin. This is her second stated interest, present clinically even though the academic division does not yet exist.

A neurology continuity clinic embedded in a federally qualified health center in historic East Austin. 'The residency offers a continuity clinic location with CommUnityCare, an organization dedicated to helping underserved residents of Austin gain access to health care. This clinic is embedded in the primary care setting in historic East Austin' - the Sandra Joy Anderson Community Health & Wellness Center, 1705 E. 11th St. A specialty continuity clinic inside an FQHC is an unusual, funded structure, and it is where her fluent Spanish would do the most clinical work.

No 24-hour call, and a graded-supervision design that is written down rather than implied. 'The program has no 24-hour call.' PGY-2s carry the consult pager but 'There is an in-house night senior for the first four months of the year, during which every PGY-2 resident has the opportunity for direct observation and feedback', after which the senior and attending staff every consult by phone. 'There is dedicated staff for the neurocritical care unit 24/7, so junior residents are not expected to manage these patients overnight.' FREIDA reports home/beeper call as [0,0,10,10] - none in PGY-1 or PGY-2.

An explicit 50:50 outpatient-inpatient design, which is genuinely unusual in neurology. 'The residencies differ from many neurology training programs in that the curriculum emphasizes outpatient neurology as much as hospital-based rotations', with a stated 'Goal for 50:50 balance between outpatient and inpatient clinical responsibilities after intern year', two-week blocks, and outpatient blocks deliberately scheduled back-to-back 'to improve continuity'. For someone planning a longitudinal, clinic-based subspecialty career in MS or movement disorders, this is the right shape of training.

A daily, protected, boards-mapped didactic structure with unusually high faculty participation. Noon core curriculum every weekday, in person and on Zoom, with lecture topics 'fully prepare[d]... for the American Academy of Neurology Resident In-Training Exam and American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology board exam'; Tuesday grand rounds with CME, hybrid so residents at either hospital can attend; a thrice-weekly stroke huddle led by Steven Warach, M.D. with vascular neurology, neuroendovascular and neurocritical care in the room; a weekly epilepsy conference from basic EEG to surgical planning; 'Chief rounds', where the teaching senior selects an inpatient and a blinded faculty member examines them live in front of learners; and resident-led morning report three days a week where 'More than 25 faculty and learners tune in'. Lecture time is protected by attendings covering pagers and outpatient residents being excused from clinic.

Benefits that are materially better than the salary line suggests. On top of the AY2026-27 PGY-1 salary of $69,528 (rising to $77,629 in PGY-4) and 15 vacation plus 10 sick days, the neurology program specifically adds meal cards covering breakfast, lunch and dinner every day; an education fund for books, board exams, journals, meetings and laptops; 50% retirement matching on up to 6% of gross income; free hospital garage parking plus transportation home for post-call residents who do not feel safe driving; and a required national conference reimbursed up to $1,500 for registration, three hotel nights, travel and meals. Institutionally: USMLE Step 3 and in-training exams paid, up to $1,000 once for board registration or prep, a one-time six-week paid parental/medical/caregiver leave available from day one, and free parking at all Ascension hospitals.

'The residencies differ from many neurology training programs in that the curriculum emphasizes outpatient neurology as much as hospital-based rotations', with a stated 'Goal for 50:50 balance between outpatient and inpatient clinical responsibilities after intern year', two-week blocks, and outpatient blocks deliberately scheduled back-to-back 'to improve continuity'. For someone planning a longitudinal, clinic-based subspecialty career in MS or movement disorders, this is the right shape of training.

A daily, protected, boards-mapped didactic structure with unusually high faculty participation. Noon core curriculum every weekday, in person and on Zoom, with lecture topics 'fully prepare[d]... for the American Academy of Neurology Resident In-Training Exam and American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology board exam'; Tuesday grand rounds with CME, hybrid so residents at either hospital can attend; a thrice-weekly stroke huddle led by Steven Warach, M.D. with vascular neurology, neuroendovascular and neurocritical care in the room; a weekly epilepsy conference from basic EEG to surgical planning; 'Chief rounds', where the teaching senior selects an inpatient and a blinded faculty member examines them live in front of learners; and resident-led morning report three days a week where 'More than 25 faculty and learners tune in'. Lecture time is protected by attendings covering pagers and outpatient residents being excused from clinic.

Benefits that are materially better than the salary line suggests. On top of the AY2026-27 PGY-1 salary of $69,528 (rising to $77,629 in PGY-4) and 15 vacation plus 10 sick days, the neurology program specifically adds meal cards covering breakfast, lunch and dinner every day; an education fund for books, board exams, journals, meetings and laptops; 50% retirement matching on up to 6% of gross income; free hospital garage parking plus transportation home for post-call residents who do not feel safe driving; and a required national conference reimbursed up to $1,500 for registration, three hotel nights, travel and meals. Institutionally: USMLE Step 3 and in-training exams paid, up to $1,000 once for board registration or prep, a one-time six-week paid parental/medical/caregiver leave available from day one, and free parking at all Ascension hospitals.

The Chair AND Program Director is herself a movement-disorders fellowship-trained neurologist (Shilpa Chitnis, MD, PhD, FAAN - Movement Disorders fellowship, Louisiana State University), and she is joined by two more movement-disorders-trained attendings: George Plotkin, MD, PhD (MIT PhD; MGH residency; MGH fellowship in neuromuscular and movement disorders; sole listed practice 'Movement disorders') and Rani Priyanka Vasireddy, MD, MHA (Movement Disorders fellowship, University of Kentucky; DBS and botulinum toxin for dystonia, blepharospasm, sialorrhea and spasticity). Three of eleven faculty in one subspecialty, led by the PD, at a program with no fellows competing for that exposure. [faculty-staff page; individual directory bios]

A movement-disorders block is a REQUIRED elective, not an optional one. The published curriculum states 'Required electives: 1 headache, 1 movement, 2 NM/EMG, 2 EEG/epilepsy, 1 behavioral, 1 radiology reading' - and unlike many of the 'additional proposed electives', the movement block carries no 'pending approval' asterisk. [curriculum page]

Twelve elective blocks across three years (5 in PGY-2, 2 in PGY-3, 5 in PGY-4 of a 13-block year), which the program itself puts forward as its defining feature: 'we have multiple elective rotations (4-5) during PGY-2 year. We also have many electives scattered throughout the 3 years of training.' Unusual latitude for a resident who wants to concentrate in one subspecialty. [curriculum page; FREIDA field_special_features]

Two active Parkinson's-disease research protocols with named topics - 'Autonomic onset Parkinson's Disease' and 'Deep Brain Stimulation in Parkinson's Disease' - run in collaboration with UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas, alongside a functional-neurological-disorder hypnosis therapy study and the CAPTIVA stroke trial (a double-blind randomized trial of medical management for severe intracranial stenosis). [department research page]

A named, directed Dementia Center: Eric Dinnerstein, MD, FAAN (Dartmouth Hitchcock residency) is 'Director of the UT Tyler Dementia Center' and Khushboo Verma, MD, MBBS (Behavioral Neurology fellowship, STANFORD) is its Assistant Director - giving a second, genuinely staffed subspecialty line and a required behavioral-neurology elective to match. [faculty-staff page; directory bios; curriculum page]

A published, unambiguous Step 2 rule that removes any interview-stage score barrier: 'Applications will be considered, and interviews offered prior to receiving Step 2 scores, however, successful completion of Step 2 (USMLE or COMLEX) is required before the rank list is submitted' - paired with 'we do not place exclusions based on USMLE/COMLEX scores, publications, number of years since medical school graduation and research experience.' Very few programs publish both sentences. [application page]

A 100% NRMP fill rate in both years the program has existed: NRMP Program Results 2022-2026 records Quota 4 / Filled 4 in 2025 and Quota 4 / Filled 4 in 2026, with no SOAP appearance. A brand-new program that filled every seat twice. [NRMP Program Results 2022-2026]

Four residents per class and no neurology fellows anywhere in the institution (the GME office lists 12 fellowships, none in neurology), so residents are the most senior neurology learners on every service - relevant to procedural volume (EMG/NCV, EEG, botulinum toxin, DBS programming exposure) and to direct attending contact. [GME program list; current residents page]

A weekly afternoon report run personally by the Program Director and/or Dr. Plotkin ('Afternoon report with Dr. Chitnis and/or Dr. Plotkin: Fridays 1-2') on top of a protected Thursday 1-4 didactic block, journal club, RITE review and quarterly Stroke M&M - i.e. the two senior movement-disorders faculty teach a scheduled weekly session. [curriculum page]

A formal Rural track (FREIDA field_special_tracks = ['Rural', 'Academic or clinician educator']) attached to a department whose stated mission is 'advancing neurological health and well-being for the people of rural East Texas' and which is 'launching the first neurological comprehensive care center in East Texas' through philanthropic support - a concrete, funded institutional priority rather than a slogan, and the only neurology residency in East Texas. [FREIDA 2026 survey; department page]

Concrete, itemized educational funding rather than a vague stipend: a laptop for the duration of residency, PubMed and UpToDate, paid registration for certification courses such as ACLS, up to $500 toward Step 3/COMLEX 3, up to $700 toward the Texas Medical License, and up to $500 per academic year for books - plus 20 vacation days and 12 sick days, and resident medical and dental coverage with no premium. Ground-floor program with a documented, verifiable start date: NRMP's March 2026 Program Results show Doctors Hospital at Renaissance-TX Neurology with NO positions offered in 2022, 2023, 2024 or 2025 and its first-ever offering in 2026 - 4 categorical (2353180C0) and 2 reserved (2353180R0), all 6 filled. An applicant joins a program with two classes total and helps set its culture, rather than inheriting one.

Demonstrated IMG access, not just stated openness: 6 of 6 current residents are international medical graduates, from Guyana, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Pakistan, Jordan and Mexico (x2). Zero US MD and zero US DO residents. Combined with J-1 sponsorship through ECFMG, no USCE requirement published, no prior GME required, and a 3-letter minimum, this is a structurally IMG-accessible program.

MS and neuroimmunology depth that is rare outside academic centres: DHR Health's MS Center was designated a Comprehensive MS Center by the National Multiple Sclerosis Society in June 2025 - 'the first and only center in the Rio Grande Valley', with the nearest previous one in San Antonio. It cares for roughly 600 MS patients and also treats NMOSD and myasthenia gravis.

The Program Director IS the subspecialist: Roberto Cruz Saldana, MD (R. Alejandro Cruz, MD) is fellowship-trained in Neuroimmunology and MS at UT Austin Dell Medical School, is DHR Health's neurology medical director, and is described by DHR as the only fellowship-trained neuroimmunologist in the Rio Grande Valley. Residents train directly under the person running the region's only comprehensive MS programme.

A dedicated Neuroimmunology Clinic block in EVERY senior year - PGY-2 block 5, PGY-3 block 4, PGY-4 block 4 - per the published 2026-2027 block schedule. Three separate immersions in neuroimmunology across training is a structural commitment most neurology curricula do not make.

Epilepsy infrastructure to match: DHR Health achieved national accreditation in May 2026 establishing 'the First and Only Comprehensive Epilepsy Center in South Texas', and core faculty member Leonel Estofan, MD is described by DHR as the only fellowship-trained adult and adolescent epilepsy physician in the Rio Grande Valley. Residents get dedicated Epilepsy Clinic/EEG blocks in PGY-3 and PGY-4.

Serious neurocritical care and stroke volume: the first Joint Commission Comprehensive Stroke Center in the region, an 8-bed neurological ICU plus a 12-bed neuro step-down unit, inside a 518-bed Level I trauma centre with 25,942 annual admissions. Residents rotate Neurology ICU/Neurosurgery in ALL FOUR years, plus a medical ICU block in PGY-1.

A genuine 4+1 continuity clinic structure, published explicitly: 'Block = A 4 week-rotation + 1 week of continuity clinic', with PGY-2 through PGY-4 residents dedicating one week of every 5-week block to neurology clinic for 10 clinic weeks annually and a minimum of 40 half-days of clinic per year. PGY-1s run the same model in internal medicine clinic.

Research is required, not optional: FREIDA records field_research_rotation = 'Required', and the block schedule carries a dedicated Research block at PGY-3. A named movement-disorders program with a named medical director who is also residency core faculty: Mazen Elkurd, II, DO, whose official BSWH profile states he 'holds the position of Medical Director of the Baylor University Medical Center Movement Disorders Program', with a movement disorders fellowship at UT Southwestern (2020) and a profile that explicitly notes involvement in 'education of medical students and residents'. A second fellowship-trained movement-disorders neurologist, Vasanthi Gomathinayagam, MD (MedStar-Georgetown fellowship, 2022), does deep brain stimulator programming and botulinum toxin injections at the same Dallas clinic. Movement disorders is named on the residency page as one of the subspecialty clinics residents rotate through.

34 weeks of dedicated outpatient neurology subspecialty clinic across PGY-2 through PGY-4 (12 + 10 + 12 weeks), plus a half-day continuity clinic every year from PGY-2 to PGY-4 -- an unusually large outpatient allocation for a 4-year neurology program, and the mechanism by which a resident reaches the movement-disorders clinic repeatedly rather than once.

Joint Commission-era Comprehensive Stroke Center with published, auditable volumes: in 2023, 125 patients treated with thrombolytics and 84 treated with mechanical endovascular reperfusion; 91.9% TICI 2b/3 successful reperfusion; median 99 minutes from arrival to procedure initiation; AHA/ASA Get With The Guidelines-Stroke Gold Plus and Target: Stroke Honor Roll-Elite with 97.3% of patients receiving thrombolytics within 60 minutes. Residents get 18 weeks of stroke service across PGY-2 to PGY-4, with a named stroke medical director (Dion Graybeal, MD) on the core faculty and 11 of 38 faculty tagged in vascular neurology.

A Level IV comprehensive epilepsy center -- the highest National Association of Epilepsy Centers designation -- with an inpatient EMU; residents spend 4 weeks on Epilepsy/EMU/EEG in PGY-2 and 4 more in PGY-3, and four core faculty carry epilepsy or clinical neurophysiology tags.

20 weeks of formal teleneurology across PGY-2 to PGY-4 inside the Baylor Scott & White Teleneurology Network, 'which includes Telestroke and Teleneurohospitalist services across several BSWH facilities' -- a distinct, scheduled, credit-bearing block rather than incidental coverage, and a marketable skill; the associate program director, Jennifer Rasmussen-Winkler, MD, is herself the Medical Director of Telestroke.

A UCNS-accredited Headache Medicine fellowship on site taking one fellow per year, with a named headache-medicine core faculty member (Avery Saporito, MD) and a BUMC Headache Center -- an in-house subspecialty fellowship that a resident can observe, rotate with, and apply to.

30 weeks of elective time across PGY-2 to PGY-4 (8 + 12 + 10) against a published 14-item elective menu that names multiple sclerosis, neurocritical care, clinical neurophysiology, interventional neuroradiology, neuro-oncology, neuromuscular disease and research -- among the more elective-heavy schedules in the set.

The program director speaks Spanish. Haseeb Abdul Rahman, MD's official BSWH profile lists 'English, Urdu, Punjabi, Hindi, Spanish'; core faculty behavioral neurologist Claudia Regina Padilla, MD lists 'English and Spanish' and staffs the Cognitive and Behavioral Neurology Clinic that residents rotate through. Two of the 38 named faculty speak Spanish, and one of them runs the program.

NAEC LEVEL 4 EPILEPSY CENTER, certified 3 April 2026 - the highest designation the National Association of Epilepsy Centers awards, held jointly by Texas Tech Health El Paso and University Medical Center of El Paso, the first such designation in the Borderplex and the only Level 4 centre in El Paso County. Residents spend 2 months in the Epilepsy Monitoring Unit in PGY-3 and another month in PGY-4, and the department's epilepsy faculty (Sushma Reddy Yerram, M.D., ABPN Epilepsy and Clinical Neurophysiology, Rochester-trained) runs medically-refractory epilepsy surgical evaluation. The department also holds an epilepsy services contract with the Texas Department of State Health Services continuously since 1990.

THE REGION'S ONLY COMPREHENSIVE STROKE CENTER, AT A COUNTY SAFETY-NET HOSPITAL. UMC of El Paso is 'home to our region's only Level 1 Stroke Center and Joint Commission-certified Comprehensive Stroke Center' and 'the only Level 1 Trauma Center in a 270-mile radius', with 293 beds, an average daily census of 269, 71,624 ED visits and 15,518 admissions a year. The department opened, in collaboration with UMC, 'the first neurocritical care unit fully staffed by neurointensivists' in the region. Residents get 4 months of Neuro ICU and Stroke Service in PGY-2 alone.

FOUR NEUROVASCULAR/NEUROINTERVENTIONAL FACULTY AND AN IN-HOUSE NEUROENDOVASCULAR SERVICE, unusual for a four-per-year program: Cruz-Flores (ABPN Vascular Neurology, UCNS Neuro-Imaging and Neuro-critical Care), Rodriguez (vascular + endovascular surgical, Minnesota), Maud (vascular + ESN, Minnesota; ABPN Neurology, Vascular Neurology and Neurocritical Care) and Piriyawat (stroke/vascular, UT Houston). Neurointervention is an explicit PGY-4 elective.

A UCNS-TRACK INTERVENTIONAL NEUROLOGY FELLOWSHIP is run by the department (2 years, PD Alberto Maud, M.D., sites UMC, Las Palmas Medical Center and El Paso Children's Hospital), so residents train alongside a neuroendovascular fellow - while, because the department runs NO epilepsy, neuromuscular or neurocritical care fellowship, residents do not compete with fellows for cases in the department's three strongest clinical areas.

THE ONLY MULTIDISCIPLINARY ALS CLINIC IN THE BORDERPLEX, described by the department as 'the only one of its kind in the Borderplex Region', led by Isabel Victoria Narvaez Correa, M.D. with physical therapists, speech therapists, dieticians, social workers and respiratory therapists. Residents get 2 months of Neuromuscular Medicine and EMG in PGY-3.

85% FELLOWSHIP-OR-FACULTY PLACEMENT ACROSS 20 PUBLISHED GRADUATES (2015-2024): 17 of 20 went to subspecialty fellowship or an academic post, at Baylor College of Medicine, NYU (x2), Emory, University of Miami, University of Chicago, Rush, University of Florida, UT Southwestern (x3), UTHealth Houston, VCU, University of Houston and University of South Carolina. Two graduates returned to this department as faculty (Narvaez Correa, Ghatali) - a 10% self-retention rate.

CATEGORICAL FOUR-YEAR STRUCTURE WITH 4 MONTHS OF NEUROLOGY IN THE INTERN YEAR. The program converted from advanced to categorical (July 2024 or July 2025 - the site gives both dates) so there is no separate preliminary-year match to run, and both published PGY-1 tracks give 4 months of neurology, one month above the ACGME minimum, alongside ICU (2 months), IM wards (2), CCU (1) and either IM fellowship consults (3) or consults plus emergency medicine.

A DECEMBER 1 DEADLINE WITH REVIEW BEGINNING IN EARLY OCTOBER - roughly a week to ten days later than the specialty norm (the OPDA guide gives 23 September 2026 as the date programs begin reviewing for 2026-2027) and with an interview window running to mid-January or early February. For an applicant whose Step 2 CK score arrives mid-October 2026, this calendar is materially more forgiving than most.

THE ONLY ACADEMIC NEUROLOGY GROUP WITHIN A 500-MILE RADIUS and the largest neurology practice in the city, grown from 3 full-time staff in January 2013 to 11 physicians and 6-7 advanced practice providers today. Practically, that means no competing academic centre siphons off complex referrals: the department is the region's referral endpoint.

A NAMED PARKINSON'S CLINIC IN THE DEPARTMENT'S OUTPATIENT PORTFOLIO. The department's published list of its outpatient clinics includes 'Parkinson's Clinic: Focused care for movement disorders' alongside General Neurology, Epilepsy, Electrodiagnosis (EMG), Geriatric Neurology and Stroke clinics; Texas Tech Physicians of El Paso separately runs a weekly community 'Dance for Parkinson's' class for adults with Parkinson's disease and other movement disorders. This is the single item on this list most relevant to a movement-disorders-interested applicant, and it is also the weakest - see domain 16 for the significant caveats.

CROSS-INSTITUTIONAL CHILD NEUROLOGY ROTATION AT THREE TEXAS ACADEMIC CENTRES. The 3-month PGY-3 child neurology block is done at TTUHSC Amarillo, UT Health San Antonio, or BAYLOR COLLEGE OF MEDICINE IN HOUSTON - a published, funded rotation that can put a resident in Houston for a quarter of a year, which is materially relevant to an applicant with family in Houston.

BILINGUAL CLINICAL FACULTY DOCUMENTED PROVIDER-BY-PROVIDER BY THE INSTITUTION: 4 of the 9 neurology physicians list Spanish in the institution's own provider directory (Cruz-Flores, Rodriguez, Maud, Acosta-Corrales) and 5 of 9 trained in Spanish-speaking countries; institution-wide, 64 of 236 Texas Tech Physicians providers (27.1%) list Spanish, and the neurology service's advanced practice providers are almost entirely El Paso natives or from Chihuahua with long UMC ICU backgrounds.

NAEC LEVEL 4 EPILEPSY CENTER, certified 3 April 2026 - the highest designation the National Association of Epilepsy Centers awards, held jointly by Texas Tech Health El Paso and University Medical Center of El Paso, the first such designation in the Borderplex and the only Level 4 centre in El Paso County. Residents spend 2 months in the Epilepsy Monitoring Unit in PGY-3 and another month in PGY-4, and the department's epilepsy faculty (Sushma Reddy Yerram, M.D., ABPN Epilepsy and Clinical Neurophysiology, Rochester-trained) runs medically-refractory epilepsy surgical evaluation. The department also holds an epilepsy services contract with the Texas Department of State Health Services continuously since 1990.

THE REGION'S ONLY COMPREHENSIVE STROKE CENTER, AT A COUNTY SAFETY-NET HOSPITAL. UMC of El Paso is 'home to our region's only Level 1 Stroke Center and Joint Commission-certified Comprehensive Stroke Center' and 'the only Level 1 Trauma Center in a 270-mile radius', with 293 beds, an average daily census of 269, 71,624 ED visits and 15,518 admissions a year. The department opened, in collaboration with UMC, 'the first neurocritical care unit fully staffed by neurointensivists' in the region. Residents get 4 months of Neuro ICU and Stroke Service in PGY-2 alone.

FOUR NEUROVASCULAR/NEUROINTERVENTIONAL FACULTY AND AN IN-HOUSE NEUROENDOVASCULAR SERVICE, unusual for a four-per-year program: Cruz-Flores (ABPN Vascular Neurology, UCNS Neuro-Imaging and Neuro-critical Care), Rodriguez (vascular + endovascular surgical, Minnesota), Maud (vascular + ESN, Minnesota; ABPN Neurology, Vascular Neurology and Neurocritical Care) and Piriyawat (stroke/vascular, UT Houston). Neurointervention is an explicit PGY-4 elective.

A UCNS-TRACK INTERVENTIONAL NEUROLOGY FELLOWSHIP is run by the department (2 years, PD Alberto Maud, M.D., sites UMC, Las Palmas Medical Center and El Paso Children's Hospital), so residents train alongside a neuroendovascular fellow - while, because the department runs NO epilepsy, neuromuscular or neurocritical care fellowship, residents do not compete with fellows for cases in the department's three strongest clinical areas.

THE ONLY MULTIDISCIPLINARY ALS CLINIC IN THE BORDERPLEX, described by the department as 'the only one of its kind in the Borderplex Region', led by Isabel Victoria Narvaez Correa, M.D. with physical therapists, speech therapists, dieticians, social workers and respiratory therapists. Residents get 2 months of Neuromuscular Medicine and EMG in PGY-3.

GROUND-FLOOR PROGRAM BUILDING: the residency enrolled its first-ever class in 2025, so a 2027 entrant is still among the founding cohorts. The inaugural resident Dr. Fidel Moreno is quoted on this directly: 'We are not only training to become neurologists, but we are also helping to build something new from the ground up... This is a rare privilege that few trainees across the country experience, and it's an opportunity to shape a positive and enduring culture of learning for those who follow.' (UTRGV Newsroom, 2025-11-03)

EXCEPTIONALLY SMALL AND HIGH-ATTENTION: 2 residents per year, with an actual current census of 2 residents total (UTRGV GME Resident Directory, 2026-09-11) and a FREIDA-reported faculty/resident ratio of 0.6:1. Individual teaching is a stated program goal -- 'Individualized teaching that focuses on a balance of clinical knowledge and anatomical localization' (Program Description).

NEUROBEHAVIORAL MEDICINE AS THE STATED PROGRAMMATIC STRENGTH: the residency sits inside a single combined Department of Neuro & Behavioral Health spanning Neurology, Neuroscience and Psychiatry, alongside a Psychiatry residency. The founding PD: 'Our strength is in neurobehavioral medicine. We're bringing together neurology, psychiatry and neuroscience. Physician residents will be immersed in multidisciplinary care.' (UTRGV Newsroom, 2025-11-03; UTRGV Neuro & Behavioral Health department page)

REAL DEMENTIA / MINORITY-AGING RESEARCH INFRASTRUCTURE IN THE SAME DEPARTMENT: the Alzheimer's Disease Resource Center for Minority Aging Research (directed by Gladys E. Maestre, MD, PhD), a Memory and Aging Center, the UTRGV Institute of Neuroscience, and a South Texas Alzheimer's Research Center -- all organizationally adjacent to the residency, with the program's neurologist documented as joining Dr. Maestre's team. (UTRGV SOM directory; UT Health RGV provider bio)

CONTEMPORARY ANTI-AMYLOID THERAPY EXPOSURE: the program's core neurologist, Dr. Carlos Martinez-Menendez, helped oversee an infusion suite administering LEQEMBI (lecanemab) on FDA approval in 2023 and monitored patients in the TRAILBLAZER trials leading to donanemab's 2024 approval -- unusual, current disease-modifying-therapy experience to learn from at a small program. (UT Health RGV provider profile)

HCA STROKE AND NEUROENDOVASCULAR VOLUME AT TWO CITIES: the residency is a collaboration with HCA Healthcare Gulf Coast Division placing residents at Rio Grande Regional Hospital (McAllen) and Valley Regional Medical Center (Brownsville), whose 'neurologists bring expertise in neuroendovascular services and high-quality stroke care.' (UTRGV Newsroom, 2025-11-03; program Training Facilities page)

CURRICULUM EXPLICITLY BUILT AROUND A HIGH-DISPARITY POPULATION: the program writes in its own FREIDA profile, 'The population is close to 90% of Hispanic descent. Income per capita shows significant income disparity in this region. Medical resources are limited. The curriculum is tailored to serve the community.' (FREIDA, Last Updated 8/20/2026)

UNUSUALLY LATE-FRIENDLY STEP 2 CK TIMING: 'Applications will be considered, and interviews offered prior to receiving Step 2 scores. However, successful completion of Step 2 (USMLE or COMLEX) is required before ranking.' Combined with a published minimum of 220 -- well below the national neurology mean -- this is materially more accessible than most programs. (Application & Selection page)

ALL-VIRTUAL INTERVIEWS, NO TRAVEL COST: 'we will conduct all residency interviews virtually for the 2026 application season', corroborated by FREIDA's 'Applicant Interview Format: Virtual'. FREIDA also notes the program 'Does not offer open house or second look', so there is no hidden in-person expectation. (Application & Selection page; FREIDA 8/20/2026)

ACADEMIC / CLINICIAN-EDUCATOR TRACK PLUS FLEXIBILITY: FREIDA reports an 'Academic or clinician educator track: Yes', a 'Curriculum to develop health systems leadership skills (e.g., QI project leadership, community/organizational advocacy): Yes', off-campus electives, and that the program 'Offers additional training or educational experience beyond accredited length: Yes'. Teaching is also a written program objective ('Experience in the teaching of neurology to colleagues and students... by means of formal presentation and publication'). (FREIDA 8/20/2026; Program Description)

STRONG REGIONAL RETENTION IF SOUTH TEXAS PRACTICE IS THE GOAL: 'Since 2016, UTRGV has trained more than 400 resident physicians, with more than half choosing to remain in Texas and a significant portion staying in the Valley.' Entry is categorical at PGY-1, so there is no separate preliminary-year match to manage. (UTRGV Newsroom, 2025-11-03; FREIDA 'PGY-1 Position Type(s) Offered: Categorical positions')

HOUSTON TEXAS MEDICAL CENTER ROTATIONS ARE BUILT INTO THE CURRICULUM. Residents spend two months at MD Anderson Cancer Center in the Texas Medical Center during PGY-2 and PGY-3 (acute neurology consult service, inpatient neuro-oncology service, neuro-oncology outpatient clinic; gliomas, meningiomas, vestibular schwannomas, CNS lymphoma, metastatic disease, chemotherapy and radiation neurotoxicity, experimental therapies), and rotate at Texas Children's Hospital in the Texas Medical Center during PGY-3/PGY-4 (the program states two months on one page and one month on another). For an applicant whose family is in Houston, this is roughly three to four months of residency spent physically in Houston, not a marketing claim.

BOTH OF HER STATED SUBSPECIALTY INTERESTS HAVE A NAMED DIVISION CHIEF AND A REQUIRED CLINIC ROTATION. Laura Wu, MD, PhD is Chief of the Movement Disorders Division (Baylor College of Medicine movement disorders fellowship; DBS and botulinum toxin expertise), and Michlene Passeri, MD is Chief of the Neuroimmunology Division (University of Colorado MS and Neuroimmunology fellowship; Barrow Neurological Institute residency and chief resident). The 'Movement Disorders Clinic, including Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) Clinic' and the 'Neuroimmunology/MS Clinic' are both listed among the REQUIRED PGY-2 subspecialty clinics, not as optional electives.

A SECOND FELLOWSHIP-TRAINED MOVEMENT DISORDERS NEUROLOGIST WITH A NAMED FELLOWSHIP DIRECTORSHIP. Dhanya Vijayakumar, MD, PhD, FANA (Weill Cornell Medicine-Qatar 2011, VCU neurology residency 2015, Baylor College of Medicine movement disorders fellowship 2017, Dystonia Medical Research Foundation grantee) joined in June 2024 and is titled Director of the Movement Disorders Fellowship Program, which UTMB describes as being launched. Two Baylor-trained movement disorders specialists in a 19-physician department is a deep bench for that subspecialty at this scale.

A CONTINUITY NEUROLOGY CLINIC THAT STARTS IN THE PGY-1 YEAR. The program states 'A distinctive feature of our program is the continuity neurology clinic, which begins in the PGY-1 year', and the weekly half-day continuity clinic continues through PGY-2 with the resident managing their own patient panel. This matches a stated longitudinal-neurology interest directly and is earlier than the common PGY-2 start.

AN IN-HOUSE PGY-1 YEAR RUN BY THE NEUROLOGY PROGRAM, INCLUDING 2.5 MONTHS OF INPATIENT NEUROLOGY AND A NEUROLOGY 'BOOT CAMP'. The PGY-1 is a categorical internal-medicine-based year inside this program, spent entirely on the Galveston campus, ending with a boot camp of introductory neurology lectures and hands-on neurologic procedural training before PGY-2 begins.

A 14-BED DEDICATED NEUROCRITICAL CARE UNIT AND COMPREHENSIVE STROKE CENTER DESIGNATION. The NCCU was established in 2013 and moved into Jennie Sealy Hospital (opened April 2016, $438 million, 310+ rooms) in 2016; the program states UTMB 'is among the few in the nation with a dedicated neuro-critical care unit'. Residents work alongside a neurocritical care fellow, a stroke fellow and a neurophysiology fellow on three different services.

A 178-BED STATEWIDE CORRECTIONAL TERTIARY HOSPITAL ON CAMPUS WITH A WEEKLY RESIDENT NEUROLOGY CLINIC AND A WEEKLY NEUROLOGY TELEMEDICINE CLINIC. TDCJ Hospital Galveston 'serves as the tertiary care hospital of the prison inmates for the entire State of Texas'. This is a specific, unusual, named clinical asset and it also gives residents structured teleneurology experience.

FELLOWSHIP AND FACULTY PLACEMENT OF ROUGHLY 44 OF 45 GRADUATES ACROSS 2014-2024, with named destinations including Mayo Clinic (x2), Yale (x2), Stanford, Beth Israel Deaconess/Harvard, Johns Hopkins, Weill Cornell, NYU (x2), Mount Sinai (x2), Emory (x4), Memorial Sloan Kettering, MD Anderson, Michigan, Pittsburgh, Georgetown, UVA, NIH, Baylor College of Medicine (x2) and UT Southwestern. Six graduates stayed at UTMB for fellowship and at least two are now UTMB neurology faculty (Ruiqing 'Linda' Sun, class of 2020; Vijaya Valaparla, class of 2024).

A FUNDED PhD PATHWAY DURING RESIDENCY PLUS TWO NAMED RESEARCH FELLOWSHIPS PER PGY-4 CLASS. Residents may take the Neurobiology of Disease (NOD) Track and 'get a PhD in neuroscience at the Mitchell Center on the Galveston Campus, during their 4 years of residency'; two PGY-4 residents each year are awarded the Texas Alzheimer's Research Care Consortium (TARCC) fellowship in dementia research. The Mitchell Center reports over $55 million in active NIH and foundation grants, a $1.6M T32, 160+ publications, 25+ graduate students and 11 postdoctoral fellows, and hosts the John Sealy Chair for Parkinson's Research (Rakez Kayed, PhD).

STRUCTURED, NAMED MENTORSHIP WITH A MONTHLY CADENCE PLUS AN ANNUAL ONE-ON-ONE WITH THE CHAIRMAN. Each resident has an assigned faculty mentor who meets with them monthly, each junior resident additionally has an assigned senior-resident mentor, and the chairman meets one-on-one with every resident yearly. The chairman also personally leads the daily Morning Report attended by all residents and faculty.

PROCEDURAL TRAINING THAT MAPS ONTO HER TWO INTERESTS. Residents 'learn and perform' Botox injections for chronic migraine, EMG-guided Botox for muscle spasticity related to stroke or multiple sclerosis, trigger point injections and occipital neuralgia blocks in the subspecialty clinics — procedures that sit inside both the movement-disorders and MS care pathways rather than adjacent to them.

A PUBLISHED STEP 2 EXPECTATION OF 200, NOT 240: the FAQ states 'A score of 200 or higher on the first attempt on Step II is preferred' - a soft preference, and one of the lowest published Step 2 expectations a competitive university program will state. Source: FREIDA survey; Application Details.

QUANTIFIED OUTPATIENT EMPHASIS, UNUSUAL FOR NEUROLOGY: 'We schedule residents for outpatient rotations a minimum of 50% of PGY2-4 blocks' (FREIDA field_special_features), with the Curriculum page adding that the residencies 'differ from many neurology training programs in that the curriculum emphasizes outpatient neurology as much as hospital-based rotations' and that two-week blocks are deliberately scheduled back-to-back for continuity. This is where longitudinal chronic-disease neurology - movement disorders, MS - is actually learned.
NO 24-HOUR CALL, stated flatly on the Curriculum page, with night float instead and home call confined to PGY-3/PGY-4 (FREIDA field_beeper_home_call = [0,0,10,10]).

A NATIONAL MS SOCIETY-DESIGNATED MS AND NEUROIMMUNOLOGY CENTER: a named adult subspecialty centre inside the Mulva Clinic, recognised by the National Multiple Sclerosis Society as a Center for Comprehensive Care, staffed by Esther Melamed MD PhD (UCLA MSTP; Stanford neurology residency and neuroimmunology fellowship; PI of the Melamed Lab; Research Director of UT Medicine's Post-COVID-19 Program) and Ethan Meltzer MD (Harvard/MGH-BWH-trained; Dell Med MS/neuroimmunology fellowship). Services include small fibre biopsy, neuro-urology, cognitive rehabilitation and neuropsychological testing. Source: Mulva Clinic page; UT Health Austin MS Center and care team; faculty bios.

A LOCAL MS/NEUROIMMUNOLOGY FELLOWSHIP TO CONTINUE INTO, asserted by both PDs in the Directors' Welcome and corroborated by Meltzer having completed it at Dell Med - so an MS-interested resident can subspecialise without leaving Austin. (Caveat: no program page; see conflicts.)

TWO STRUCTURALLY DIFFERENT TEACHING HOSPITALS, deliberately contrasted by the program: 'Ascension Seton Medical Center gives residents exposure to pure consultative neurology whereas the Dell Seton Medical Center services are a hybrid of both primary neurology patients and consults', with complex cardiac and obstetric neurology at one site and complex rheumatologic and infectious disease at the other. Source: Curriculum.

A SAFETY-NET LEVEL I TRAUMA CENTRE AS THE PRIMARY SITE: Dell Seton Medical Center at UT is Travis County's safety-net hospital, operated in partnership with Central Health (the county public hospital district), a 210-bed academic hospital and the only Level I Trauma Center for an eleven-county Central Texas region. Plus VA rotations through the Central Texas Veterans Health Care System during PGY-1 clinic weeks.

GRADUATED SUPERVISION WITH A NAMED MECHANISM, not a slogan: 'There is an in-house night senior for the first four months of the year, during which every PGY-2 resident has the opportunity for direct observation and feedback', and 'There is dedicated staff for the neurocritical care unit 24/7, so junior residents are not expected to manage these patients overnight.' Didactics are protected by attendings holding the pagers and outpatient residents being excused from clinical duty. Source: Curriculum.

CONCRETE FUNDED BENEFITS: $1,500 for one mandatory national conference (registration, three hotel nights, travel, meal per diem); 50% retirement match on up to 6% of gross; daily meal cards for three meals; free hospital-garage parking; transportation home for post-call residents who do not feel safe driving; USMLE Step 3 and in-training exam fees paid; up to $1,000 once for board exam registration or preparation. Source: Application Details FAQ; GME Salary & Benefits.

Train inside the Stanley H. Appel Department of Neurology with Dr. Stanley H. Appel himself on the active residency teaching faculty (Peggy and Gary Edwards Distinguished Chair in ALS Research). The department runs an MDA/ALSA ALS Clinic, and residents staff their own MDA clinic twice monthly on the 2nd and 4th Fridays under neuromuscular faculty, seeing motor neuron disease, Duchenne/Becker dystrophy, Charcot-Marie-Tooth, myasthenic syndromes and ataxias. Source: program page + teaching faculty directory + centers list.

Required 2-block PGY-3 neuro-oncology rotation AT MD ANDERSON CANCER CENTER, split two weeks inpatient consult/admission and two weeks in the outpatient Primary Brain Tumor clinic. Very few neurology residencies embed required training at a top-two cancer center. Source: program page.

At least nine in-house neurology fellowships to progress into without leaving the institution: Vascular Neurology (ACGME, 2 positions), Clinical Neurophysiology (ACGME), Neuromuscular Medicine (ACGME), Behavioral Neurology & Neuropsychiatry (UCNS), Neuroimaging, Movement Disorders, Neurocritical Care, Neuro-Ophthalmology, and Neuropathology. Six of these are independently confirmed by named graduates in the program's own alumni directory. Source: nine Houston Methodist GME fellowship pages + alumni directory.

A deep Movement Disorders bench for a subspecialty-focused applicant: William G. Ondo, MD (fellowship PD, nationally known in Parkinson's, essential tremor, botulinum toxin and RLS), Eugene C. Lai, MD PhD (Robert W. Hervey Chair for Parkinson's Research and Treatment), plus Billnitzer, Waln and Imbs; a dedicated Movement Disorders Clinic AND a separate Functional and Movement Disorder Surgical Program; a guaranteed PGY-2 Movement Disorders outpatient block; and procedural training in botulinum toxin, DBS management and baclofen pumps available on site. Source: faculty directory + centers list + fellowship page + program page.

Required research with real scaffolding, not a checkbox: residents receive certified training in research methods and ethics, FREIDA records the research rotation as Required, and the environment supplies 81 active clinical trials and 67 peer-reviewed publications in 2024. Source: program page + FREIDA.

Weekly PGY-3/PGY-4 longitudinal clinic at San Jose Clinic, Houston's original safety-net clinic, whose 2023 patient population was 80% Hispanic/Latino and entirely uninsured/underserved - explicitly framed by the program as 'an opportunity for autonomy in a clinical setting with limited resources', treating epilepsy, headache, Parkinson's, myasthenia, dementia, neuropathy and back pain. Houston Methodist is also a six-figure institutional donor to the clinic and holds a board seat. Source: program page + San Jose Clinic 2023 Impact Report.

Favorable teaching density: 37 named teaching faculty for 28 residents (about 1.3:1), with at least nine endowed chairs among them, in a program the PD describes as having 'a high faculty-to-resident ratio'. Ignore the registry's 0.00:1 ratio - that is a FREIDA null-sentinel artifact, not a real value. Source: teaching faculty directory + program page.

A structured leadership and educator pathway: one PGY-4 is ELECTED administrative chief resident each year and works as liaison between staff and residents while assisting in program development; every PGY-4 delivers a Houston Methodist Grand Rounds presentation on a topic of their choice; PGY-3s present basic-science lectures to the department under a research mentor; and FREIDA records a Clinician Educator track plus Health Systems Leadership and Healthcare Economics curricula. Source: program page + FREIDA.

Concrete outpatient and ICU procedural training that many neurology programs leave vague: in the PGY-4 general continuity clinic, Botox injection, occipital nerve block and lumbar puncture; in two Neuro-ICU blocks (PGY-2 and PGY-3), intubation and ventilator management, arterial and central line placement, and emergent cardioversion during CPR. Source: program page.

Academic infrastructure beyond the hospital: Weill Cornell Medical College affiliation, a new Weill Cornell neuroscience PhD program on campus, and the joint Houston Methodist-Rice University Center for Neural Systems Restoration - alongside U.S. News rankings of Best in Texas and No. 13 nationally for Neurology & Neurosurgery, and No. 1 hospital in Texas for 15 consecutive years. Source: program page + Academic Institute neuro education page.

Source: program page.

Academic infrastructure beyond the hospital: Weill Cornell Medical College affiliation, a new Weill Cornell neuroscience PhD program on campus, and the joint Houston Methodist-Rice University Center for Neural Systems Restoration - alongside U.S. News rankings of Best in Texas and No. 13 nationally for Neurology & Neurosurgery, and No. 1 hospital in Texas for 15 consecutive years. Source: program page + Academic Institute neuro education page.

Two endowed chairs in Parkinson's/neurodegeneration held by one professor (Henrik Wilms, M.D., Ph.D.): the Abraham-Tarbox Chair in Neurodegenerative Diseases and the CH-Foundation Chair in Parkinson's Disease Research - with 'Movement Disorders Neurology' as his formal practice-plan subspecialty designation.

Deep brain stimulation PROGRAMMING is performed in this clinic, documented in TTUHSC's own published patient story (Abbott Infinity system, device adjusted at each visit, ~40 percent medication reduction in a young-onset Parkinson's patient).

Current residents are first-authoring neuroimmunology papers with her: 'Acute Ischemic Stroke in the Setting of Neurosarcoidosis', Clinical Case Reports, June 2025, authors Suppakitjanusant P, Srifuengfung G, Chaisrimaneepan N, Avila M - the first two are still in the program today.

Residents first-author movement-disorders work with Wilms in serious journals: 'Mystery Case: Symptomatic isolated tongue tremor of cortical origin due to stroke', Neurology, 2020, three residents plus Wilms; and a dopamine-agonist Parkinson's case report in Clinical Neurology and Neurosurgery, 2022.

The program grows and keeps its own people: the Program Director (Jannatul Ferdous, Class of 2017, Vanderbilt epilepsy fellowship) and the Interim Chair/APD (Mirla Avila, Class of 2016) are both graduates of this residency.

No fellows anywhere in neurology at this institution - TTUHSC Lubbock runs 17 fellowships and not one is a neurology subspecialty - so residents are the senior learners on every service and no fellow layer absorbs procedures, consults or teaching.

The department owns its neurodiagnostic lab and states a deliberate strategy of unrestricted resident procedural access: 32-channel video EEG with ambulatory and long-term monitoring, EMG, NCV, evoked potentials, TCD and diagnostic ultrasound, tilt-table, autonomic testing, Humphrey visual fields and OCT, 'performed in our department by our faculty, technicians and residents'.

A full in-house neurointerventional service (Saif Bushnaq, M.D.) at a Level I trauma centre: endovascular thrombectomy, aneurysm coiling and flow diversion, AVM/DAVF/CCF embolization, carotid/intracranial/vertebral stenting, venous sinus stenting, balloon test occlusion.

Quantified catchment: the only academic neurologic centre in the Texas South Plains, 'an area larger than New England', 62 counties across West Texas, eastern New Mexico and southwestern Oklahoma, two hospitals totalling 1,300-plus beds, with AeroCare flying roughly 920 patients a year into the two systems.
No published minimum USMLE score of any kind - the Application Process page's Minimum Requirements section reads, in full, 'No minimum score requirements'.

Step 2 CK is not required at application, review, interview or ranking; institutional policy defers the pass to the end of the PGY-1 contract year, and the program itself answered 'Step 2 required for interview: no' on its June 2026 FREIDA survey.

Three-system training across genuinely different practice models in the same city: William P. Clements Jr. University Hospital (quaternary academic, on campus), Parkland Hospital (described by the department as 'one of the busiest public hospitals in the nation', UTSW's 'primary teaching facility', with 'more than 1 million patient visits each year'), and VA North Texas Health Care System (serving a 30-county area). Source: clinical-settings.html and the residency landing page.

Resident continuity clinics are physically 'housed in Parkland's ambulatory care center' - so the longitudinal outpatient panel is a public safety-net panel, not a faculty-practice panel, for all four years. Source: clinical-settings.html.

Neurology from day one of internship: the PGY-1 is an integrated internship within the Internal Medicine residency with 'Neurology Clinic weeks' every 5 weeks, 4 weeks of neurology elective, and a final-month 'Neurology Bootcamp' using shadowing, simulations and lectures before PGY-2 starts. Source: adult residency page.

X+Y block scheduling in PGY-2 ('X weeks of inpatient service followed by Y weeks of outpatient clinics') with every-5th-week continuity clinic in PGY-2 and PGY-4 - clinic is protected from inpatient conflict by design rather than squeezed around it. Source: adult residency page.

Substantial protected elective time: 6-10 weeks in PGY-2 and 12-14 weeks in PGY-4, against an unusually broad elective menu of 16+ named options including a dedicated Procedure rotation, Neurosonology, Neuromuscular ultrasound, Interventional Neuroradiology, Sports Neurology and Autonomic Disorders. Source: adult residency page.

Movement disorders depth well beyond a typical residency elective: a ten-faculty section handling '7,000 patient visits annually across 9 subspecialty clinics' (ataxia, tremor, NPH, chemodenervation, Huntington's, dystonia, neuromodulation, plus a total-care Parkinson's program), with DBS, focused ultrasound and EMG-guided botulinum toxin, an 'international cell repository for ataxia research', and 10+ active clinical studies. Movement Disorders is a required core outpatient rotation, not just an elective. Sources: movement-disorders section and fellowship pages, adult residency page.

Department Chair Elan Louis, M.D., M.S. is an internationally recognized essential tremor and movement-disorders epidemiologist who is also listed as key teaching faculty on the movement disorders fellowship - an unusual degree of chair-level subspecialty access for residents. Sources: faculty page, movement disorders fellowship page.

Neuroimmunology/MS breadth: a ten-physician section with 'Six faculty have extramural funding', running six distinct clinics under the CONQUER program (MS, NMOSD, MOGAD, transverse myelitis, autoimmune encephalitis, pediatric MS) across UTSW, Parkland and Children's, backed by a Neuroscience Biorepository. Neuroimmunology is a required core outpatient rotation, and the residency's own APD (Kyle Blackburn, M.D.) is a neuroimmunologist. Sources: MS/neuroimmunology section page, adult residency page, faculty page.

Twelve in-house fellowships covering essentially the whole specialty, meaning subspecialty electives are taught by the same faculty who run the fellowships - and this shows up in outcomes: 'More than one-half' of graduates who pursue fellowship 'have chosen UT Southwestern neurology fellowships'. Sources: fellowships page, education page.

Documented graduate outcome: 'Over the last five years, 95% of UT Southwestern's graduating neurology residents have pursued such additional post-residency training opportunities.' Source: department education page.

A fully built physician-scientist pathway rather than a nominal research track: up to 70 protected research weeks across four years (PGY1 14, PGY2 11, PGY3 15, PGY4 30), 27 funded faculty mentors, three distinct NIH-linked funding mechanisms (NINDS UE5 'UT SWANS', TARDIS for MDs without prior research training, OBI Sprouts pilot funding), K-award writing support, and $1,000/yr travel plus up to $2,500 OBI Travel Grants - sitting inside a department with '$116.7M In all research funding', '53 Active NIH grants', '1 in 4 Faculty with NIH Funding', and a Blue Ridge Institute ranking of 21. Sources: PSTP page, PSTP mentors page, department research page.

Structured non-clinical programming that is actually named and scheduled: Women In Neurology (WIN) quarterly mentorship meetings, a monthly 'Art of Neurology' series on 'interpersonal dynamics among the physician, patient, family, and community', an annual Neurology Research Day at which 'All senior Neurology Residents present', and month-long global health rotations in Zambia and Ethiopia. Source: adult residency page.

World-leading movement disorders center: the Parkinson's Disease Center and Movement Disorders Clinic, founded and directed by Joseph Jankovic, M.D., holds Center of Excellence designation from FOUR separate disease societies simultaneously — the Parkinson's Foundation, the Huntington's Disease Society of America, the Tourette Association of America, and the Wilson Disease Association. Residents get a dedicated PGY3 outpatient movement disorders rotation plus weekly Friday movement disorders video rounds. (bcm.edu movement disorders fellowship; adult residency rotations and curriculum pages)

Movement disorders research and procedural scale that is difficult to match anywhere: a clinical database of 33,000 patients with 40,000 diagnoses and a video library of 25,000 cases, over 30 ongoing clinical trials through an experimental therapeutics program, 'one of the largest botulinum toxin programs in the world', a strong DBS and neuromodulation program, and focused ultrasound (FUS) pending initiation. The fellowship itself dates to 1977. (bcm.edu movement disorders fellowship)

NMSS-designated Maxine Mesinger Multiple Sclerosis Comprehensive Care Center (founded 2003) with five full-time MS/neuroimmunology faculty under George J. Hutton, M.D., covering MS, NMOSD, MOG-antibody disease, neurosarcoidosis and autoimmune encephalitis, and participating in the NIH-funded BEAT-MS hematopoietic stem cell transplantation trial. Residents get MS outpatient blocks in PGY2 and a weekly Thursday MS Case Conference. (bcm.edu MS fellowship; BCM MS clinic page; residency didactics page)

NINE in-house Department of Neurology fellowships — Behavioral Neurology & Neuropsychiatry, Clinical Neurophysiology, Clinical Neuropsychology, Epilepsy, Movement Disorders, Multiple Sclerosis, Neurocritical Care, Neuromuscular Medicine, and Vascular Neurology — meaning nearly every subspecialty pathway exists internally. (bcm.edu Department of Neurology Education page)

A genuinely multi-system training model inside one medical center: Baylor St. Luke's (private academic; ranked #17 in Neurology and Neurosurgery by U.S. News; closed 20-bed neuro ICU, comprehensive stroke center, 4-bed EMU), Ben Taub (Harris Health county safety-net flagship; Elite Level 1 trauma center; comprehensive stroke center), the Michael E. DeBakey VA (Parkinson's Disease Research Center; Comprehensive Epilepsy Center of Excellence), MD Anderson (NCI cancer center), and Texas Children's — so a resident sees insured, indigent, veteran, oncologic and pediatric neurology populations without changing programs. (bcm.edu training locations page)

Dedicated neuro-oncology training at UT MD Anderson Cancer Center — PGY2 neuro-oncology consults and a PGY3 Primary Brain and Spine Tumor Clinic rotation. Structured resident access to a top-tier NCI comprehensive cancer center is uncommon among neurology programs. (bcm.edu adult residency rotations page)

True longitudinal continuity: 'PGY2-PGY4 residents participate in a weekly continuity clinic throughout their training with an individual panel of patients' — a personal panel followed across three years, not a rotating clinic assignment. (bcm.edu adult residency curriculum page)

Deliberately graduated leadership: PGY3 residents serve as consultation service chiefs at Ben Taub and MEDVAMC and as neuro ICU chief at Baylor St. Luke's with acute stroke call; PGY4 residents serve as inpatient service chiefs at Ben Taub and MEDVAMC. Call also decompresses across training — PGY1-2 carry front-loaded night float, while PGY3-4 are 'rarely overnight in-house' with backup call from home. (bcm.edu adult residency rotations page)

Elective breadth backed by program scale: three dedicated elective months in PGY3 plus additional PGY4 months for subspecialty or research. The program describes itself as one of the largest neurology residencies in the country, which 'enables great flexibility and freedom in electives and pursuing one's own interests'. (bcm.edu adult residency landing and rotations pages)

Scholarship is required and defined, not aspirational: every resident must produce THREE scholarship examples — journal articles, regional or national meeting posters, Case-of-the-Month presentations, or Performance Improvement projects — supported by a formal mentor assigned in PGY1. (bcm.edu adult residency curriculum page)

Protected, heavily structured didactics: mandatory daily noon conferences plus a two-hour Friday interactive block (neuroradiology, neuropathology, Case of the Week, journal clubs, movement disorders video rounds, M&M and QI), layered on top of subspecialty conferences running Monday through Thursday including epilepsy surgery conference, MS case conference, interventional neuroradiology and stroke M&M. (bcm.edu adult residency didactics page)

Program leadership is home-grown and embedded in the safety net: Program Director Corey Elam Goldsmith, M.D. completed both his internal medicine internship and his neurology residency at this program, and concurrently serves as Chief of Neurology Outpatient Clinics at Ben Taub Hospital in the Harris Health System — plus the epilepsy/neurophysiology infrastructure he came from, the NAEC Level IV Baylor Comprehensive Epilepsy Center and the Peter Kellaway Section of Neurophysiology, gives residents dedicated PGY3 EMG and EEG/EMU months. (BCM people-search profile; residency faculty page; clinical neurophysiology fellowship page; rotations page)

The sitting Neurology Residency Program Director, Sarah Horn MD, is herself a Parkinson's Disease and Movement Disorders Program faculty member - the person who reads her application and runs her training shares her stated subspecialty interest.

The Parkinson's Disease and Movement Disorders Program states it is 'the only comprehensive Movement Disorders Center in the area of South Central Texas,' with four fellowship-trained movement disorders specialists and two advanced practice providers, and holds three named national designations: Huntington Disease Society of America Center of Excellence Level 1 partner site (with UTHealth Houston), CurePSP Center of Care (2025, co-directed by Alicia Parker MD and Leila Saadatpour MD), and a Lewy Body Dementia Association Research Center of Excellence via the Biggs Institute.

The department is a National Multiple Sclerosis Society-designated Comprehensive MS Center - 'the first and only' in San Antonio and South Texas, awarded 2016, one of only eight in Texas - treating over 2,000 neuroimmunologic patients from a clinic that began with 200 patients in 2011.

A named Spanish Language Clinic operates inside the department, with 'All services, from neuropsychological assessments to counseling ... provided in Spanish' and a 2025 working partnership with the CAPAS Center 'to ensure that research and care are optimized for Hispanic/Latino families in South Texas.'

Tania Reyna MD, Chief of Neuroimmunology and MS/Neuroimmunology Fellowship Director, is a member of the National MS Society's Hispanic Latinx MS Community Collaborative - a formal national Hispanic-focused role held by the exact faculty member who would supervise an MS-interested resident.

The movement disorders research program is a Parkinson's Foundation PD GENEration Super Site and was the top recruiting site nationally in 2024 and 2025, with an explicit goal of recruiting Parkinson's patients 'particularly those from a Hispanic background,' plus a funded 'Building a Health Coach Program' study coaching 'underserved communities and Hispanic minorities with Parkinson's Disease.'

The Glenn Biggs Institute is an NIA-designated Alzheimer's Disease Research Center whose designation was renewed in 2025, making it 'the only federally designated center of its kind in Texas,' and movement disorders and behavioral neurology trainees conduct research there.

New physical plant: the Center for Brain Health opened in 2025 - five stories, 103,000 square feet, 75 exam rooms, a dedicated 12-chair non-oncology infusion suite, meditation/art/music rooms, connected to the MARC by pedestrian bridge - and houses the region's only 7-Tesla MRI.

The program publishes thirteen consecutive graduating classes (2013-2025) with each graduate's name and destination, and the record shows a real internal pipeline: Pablo Coss (2020), Leila Saadatpour (2022), Cassie Chan (2022), Andres Saenz (2022), Muhammad Abdullah (2023) and Missak Tchoulhakian (2023) are all now on this department's faculty, and Andrew Slusher (2018) returned as an Associate Program Director of this residency.

Eight departmental fellowships with eleven fellows currently in post, including two ACGME-accredited ones - Clinical Neurophysiology, which 'received ACGME accreditation with commendation for up to three CNP fellowship positions' with 10 CNP faculty, and Epilepsy, based at 'one of the largest level-4 NAEC epilepsy centers in Texas (9 epileptologists, 2 epilepsy-trained neurosurgeons, a state-of-the-art 14-bed epilepsy monitoring unit).'

Research scale is quantified, not asserted: the Department of Neurology ranked 4th in Texas and 33rd nationally in the Blue Ridge rankings with almost $10 million in NIH funding, 50 grants, 100 clinical trials, 600 research subjects and more than 30 faculty involved in research; the department reports more than 115 active clinical trials today.

Clinical partners are a Bexar County public hospital district safety-net system (University Health, third largest public health system in Texas, 716-bed University Hospital, Comprehensive Stroke Center with Gold Plus certification, Level-1 trauma center) plus the 462-bed Audie L. Murphy VA connected by sky bridge - two payer-mix-distinct training environments in walking distance of each other.

Residents outperform fellows on a fellow-level examination: 'our residents routinely score above the national mean on an EMG test which is typically only administered to fellows'. Reinforced by a required 'SAUSHEC Neurology Neurophysiology Course (PGY3)'. (health.mil program page)

A combat-setting status epilepticus simulation run without warning: the published simulation curriculum lists Acute Stroke, Brain Death Evaluation & Delivering Bad News, and 'Status Epilepticus (set in combat environment)', which 'occurs (without the residents' prior knowledge) in a deployed combat setting'. (health.mil program page)

In-house deep brain stimulation programming with a published follow-up cadence - patients seen one month post-implant, then every 3-4 months in year one, then once or twice yearly - using device-telemetry tablets that let the neurologist read local field potentials and 'steer' stimulation to the offending brainwaves. An active, named research program on early-onset Parkinson's disease in active-duty service members - deployment history, toxic-exposure testing, genetics and microbiome - which the investigators state has not been done before in this population. (jbsa.mil, 15 April 2025)

The Associate Program Director is a Mayo Clinic Arizona-trained neuroimmunologist whose clinical and research focus is MOG Antibody Disease and Multiple Sclerosis, with a publication record on monoclonal antibodies in MS and tocilizumab in MOGAD: Lt Col Paul M. Elsbernd, MD, MS, 'Staff Neurologist/Neuroimmunologist, San Antonio Military Medical Center' and APD since June 2024. (usuhs.edu profile)

Tri-site training that deliberately crosses the military/civilian/VA boundary: 13 blocks per year across Brooke Army Medical Center, the Audie L. Pathology volume from the DoD's only Level I trauma center: more than 6,000 military and civilian trauma patients a year including 750 burn patients, drawn from 22 Southwest Texas counties and 2.8 million people, co-located with the DoD's only ABA-verified burn center, its only ECMO center, and the Center for the Intrepid. 32-bed Neuro-Trauma ICU described as the largest in the area, with dedicated faculty specialized in Neurocritical Care, plus a 15-bed Neuro IMU and 12-bed Stroke IMU at Memorial Hermann-TMC (1,082 beds, Level I Trauma, Comprehensive Stroke Center).

NIH-funded R25 Research Education Program offering '6-8 months of protected research time in PGY-3/PGY-4 years under a mentor at UTHealth' PLUS '1-2 years of research support after residency or clinical fellowship training' - post-residency funding continuity is unusual and concrete.

Clinical Research Curriculum: 'a 2-year series of evening courses' covering epidemiology, biostatistics, clinical trial design, grant submission and research ethics - a structured research education spine rather than ad hoc mentorship.

UTMOVE Movement Disorders: the largest movement disorder clinic in Texas and Louisiana, over 6,000 patients across three outpatient clinics and two teaching hospitals, a DBS program described as one of the top 10 worldwide, and recipient of the Edmond J. Safra Fellowship in Movement Disorders (Michael J. Fox Foundation partnership).

A named faculty member, Raja Mehanna, MD, holds the explicit role 'Director of movement disorders curriculum for fellows and residents' - subspecialty teaching is an assigned responsibility, not incidental.

Level 4 Comprehensive Epilepsy Program (Texas Comprehensive Epilepsy Program, Samden Lhatoo, MD, FRCP) with a robust surgical program, plus a dedicated 8-week epilepsy/EEG course offered in the PGY-2 or PGY-4 year.

Huntington's Disease Society of America Center of Excellence, founded and directed by Erin Furr Stimming, MD, who is also the neurology clerkship director - with active disease-modifying HD clinical trials.

MS/Neuroimmunology division established in 1983 by Jerry S. Wolinsky, MD, with 5 clinical faculty, a dedicated MRI Analysis Center, and a fellowship running one fellow per year since 2018 whose 'last three fellows have assumed a faculty position at an academic program.'

Dual-system training by design: first two years predominantly at Memorial Hermann-TMC and UT Physicians, then senior years shifting into the Harris Health county safety-net system (LBJ Hospital, Smith Clinic), giving graded exposure to both quaternary referral and public-hospital neurology, with continuity clinic maintained throughout all four years.

Nine in-house Neurology fellowships (Clinical Neurophysiology, Epilepsy, Movement Disorders, Multiple Sclerosis, Neurocognitive Disorders, Neuroendovascular, Neurohospitalist, Neuropsychology, Vascular Neurology), with a demonstrated internal pipeline - 2 to 4 graduates per class have stayed at UTHealth for fellowship in each of the last five published classes.

Documented external fellowship placement strength: the Class of 2023 placed 10 of 10 graduates into fellowships including Brigham and Women's/Harvard (Epilepsy), UCLA (Stroke/Vascular), University of Pennsylvania (StrokeNet/Vascular), University of Pittsburgh (Stroke), NewYork-Presbyterian/Weill Cornell (Clinical Neurophysiology), USC (MS) and Dartmouth Hitchcock (Clinical Neurophysiology).
